id: A Song of a Young Lady to Her Ancient Lover

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Ancient person, for whom I All the flattering youth defy, Long be it ere thou grow old, Aching, shaking, crazy, cold; But still continue as thou art, Ancient person of my heart. On thy withered lips and dry, Which like barren furrows lie, Brooding kisses I will pour Shall thy youthful [heat] restore (Such kind showers in autumn fall, And a second spring recall); Nor from thee will ever part, Ancient person of my heart. Thy nobler part, which but to name In our sex would be counted shame, By age’s frozen grasp possessed, From [his] ice shall be released, And soothed by my reviving hand, In former warmth and vigor stand. All a lover’s wish can reach For thy joy my love shall teach, And for they pleasure shall improve All that art can add to love. Yet still I love thee without art, Ancient person of my heart.

outputs.L2:
Old beloved, for your sake I reject every charming young admirer. May many years pass before age makes you frail—before pain, trembling, confusion, and coldness overtake you. Remain just as you are, aged darling of my heart.

Upon your dry, wrinkled lips, lying like empty plowed fields, I will shower lingering kisses. Those kisses will bring back your youthful warmth, like gentle autumn rain that calls forth a second spring. I will never leave you, old beloved of my heart.

That more intimate part of you, which women would be ashamed even to mention, may now be held in age’s icy grip; yet it shall be freed from that frost. Comforted by my life-giving touch, it will regain its former heat and strength.

Whatever a lover can desire for your happiness, my affection will provide. For your pleasure, it will refine and heighten everything skill can add to love. And still, beyond all practiced arts, I love you truly, aged beloved of my heart.
outputs.L3:
The speaker declares a clear preference for an older beloved over any youthful admirers. Rather than being drawn to the freshness or beauty of the young, the speaker values the beloved as they are and chooses them with affection and loyalty. This choice suggests that the speaker’s love is not based merely on outward youth, but on deeper attachment, tenderness, and admiration.

At the same time, the speaker wishes that the beloved could remain unchanged and be spared the physical and emotional pains that come with aging. There is a desire to preserve the beloved’s present self, to protect them from decline, and to keep them free from suffering. This wish reveals both compassion and a longing to resist time’s effects.

The speaker also promises to offer affection that can revive and comfort the beloved. Through kisses and loving attention, the speaker imagines restoring the beloved’s youthful warmth, as though love itself has the power to renew life and vitality. These gestures are presented not simply as passion, but as acts of care meant to soothe and strengthen the beloved.

Most importantly, the speaker vows never to abandon the beloved because of age. Their devotion is steadfast, and they insist that aging will not lessen their commitment. Instead of turning away, the speaker pledges constancy, remaining loyal even as time changes the beloved’s appearance or strength.

Overall, the speaker presents their love as devoted, skillful, and sincere. Their affection is not shallow or temporary, but thoughtful and enduring. They portray themselves as someone capable of loving with tenderness, experience, and faithfulness, offering the beloved not only desire but also reassurance, comfort, and lasting commitment.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a tender meditation on devotion to an aging beloved, showing love not as something weakened by time, but as a force that continues to nourish, comfort, and renew. Rather than focusing only on the physical signs of age, the speaker responds to the beloved with intimacy and care, using restorative imagery that suggests warmth returning to the body, youth briefly revived, and desire kept alive despite decline. This creates a deeply affectionate portrait of love as both emotional loyalty and physical tenderness.

At the heart of the poem is the idea that true affection does not depend on youth, beauty, or vitality. The beloved may be aging, but the speaker’s devotion remains constant, even strengthened by the awareness of time passing. Love is presented as something capable of resisting coldness, weakness, and decay; it becomes a source of renewal, almost as if the speaker’s tenderness can restore life and energy to the beloved. Through this imagery, the poem suggests that intimacy has the power to heal and preserve what age threatens to diminish.

The poem’s central message is therefore one of enduring commitment. It argues that genuine love survives beyond physical decline and continues to find beauty, desire, and value in the beloved. By portraying love as loyal, warming, and rejuvenating, the poem defies the usual association of aging with loss. Instead, it presents affection as a sustaining power—one that honors the aging body while also imagining the possibility of renewed passion and vitality.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an 18th-century-style erotic love poem addressed to an elderly beloved, using the refrain “Ancient person of my heart.”
counterfactuals.output:
**Ancient person of my heart,**  
Though silver time thy temples crown,  
Thy glance can bid my reason start  
And loose my guarded senses down.  

No rose of June, in haste to die,  
Can match the grace thy years impart;  
I read whole summers in thine eye,  
**Ancient person of my heart.**  

Thy hand, so learned in tenderness,  
Doth wake what younger hands but mar;  
Each wrinkle is a map I press,  
A road to some remembered star.  

Come, let the candles blush and lean,  
Let night draw close its velvet art;  
Age hath not cooled, but made more keen,  
**Ancient person of my heart.**  

For love, like wine in cellars deep,  
Grows richer under dust and dark;  
And I would taste, and tasting keep,  
The fire that glimmers in thy spark.  

Then rest thy years against my breast,  
Nor fear what fleeting youths depart;  
The oldest flame may burn the best,  
**Ancient person of my heart.**
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a rhymed mock-sentimental poem in antique diction where the speaker promises to revive an old lover’s youth through affection.
counterfactuals.output:
**A Fond Receipt for Wither’d Charms**

O come, my Phyllis, cease thy sighs,  
Nor count the winters in thine eyes;  
Though Time hath thinn’d thy auburn hair,  
My kisses shall replant it there.  

Though roses fled thy cheek of snow,  
One amorous glance shall bid them grow;  
And if thy dimples be decayed,  
I’ll dig them new with tender spade.  

Thy voice, once sweet as linnet’s lay,  
Now creaks like casements in decay;  
Yet let me whisper, “Thou art mine,”  
And straight ’twill ring like musick fine.  

Thy step, that trips no more the green,  
Shall dance, if I be but between;  
I’ll lend my arm, my heart, my cane,  
And make thee twenty-two again.  

Then chide not Fate, nor fret at years,  
Nor pickle all thy charms in tears;  
For Love, that quack of high renown,  
Can paint the lily, rouge the brown.  

So take my vow, my ancient dove:  
I’ll physic thee with draughts of love;  
And though we both be past our prime,  
We’ll cheat the parish-clock and Time.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
